strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem: supporting heterogeneous quantization configurations without fine-tuning and storing a separate LoRA adapter for every configuration.
The configuration-conditioned r-by-r transformation is lightweight and potentially useful, while the combination with configuration search offers a coherent high-level approach.

The evaluation covers four GLUE tasks, three language-model sizes from 1.5B to 7B, multiple LoRA ranks, unseen configurations, zero-shot tasks, and ablations of configuration search and Pareto segmentation.
Reported GLUE results are promising: CoA-LoRA generally improves over Shared-LoRA and often matches or exceeds separately trained Q-LoRA/LQ-LoRA at the evaluated bit budgets.
The motivation and main workflow are presented clearly, and the figures communicate the intended accuracy-efficiency trade-off effectively.
weaknesses: The method is not specified sufficiently to establish technical soundness or reproducibility. The architecture and parameter count of the configuration-aware model, embedding dimensions, treatment of categorical configuration variables, optimizer and batch settings, and whether the base LoRA matrices are jointly trained with theta are missing. Equation (3) optimizes only theta, although the method appears to require learning L1 and L2 as well.

The discrete search procedure is mathematically unclear. Equations (7)-(8) perturb continuous embeddings and apply signed coordinate steps, but the paper does not explain how these operations map back to valid categorical NF configurations. It is also unclear how a high-dimensional GP is fitted reliably from roughly 50 observations or updated during cyclic training.

There are serious internal inconsistencies. Appendix Eq. (11) adds L1 and L2 despite incompatible dimensions, rather than multiplying them. Its binary encoding and one-hot constraint do not represent the multivalued five-variable space described in Table 1. The main text defines the Pareto objectives as task performance and bit-width, whereas Appendix B says the second objective is accuracy or perplexity. Algorithm 1 also appears to fit the GP only once and omits an assignment in its configuration update.

The empirical motivation for transforming L2 is contradictory. Appendix C.1 states that configuration-specific information is primarily encoded in L1 while shared information is in L2, yet the proposed method transforms L2. This conflicts with the stated design rationale and is not resolved experimentally through an L1-versus-L2 adjustment ablation.

Hypervolume comparisons are potentially unfair: CoA-LoRA contributes around 50 points spanning 2.5-6.25 bits, while Q-LoRA and LQ-LoRA contribute only four points spanning 2.5-4 bits. Since hypervolume rewards coverage, the metric can favor CoA-LoRA independently of accuracy. A comparison on identical configurations/ranges, or interpolated envelopes with uncertainty, is required.

The strongest one-to-one baselines are evaluated on only four configurations, with no random-search or stronger multi-configuration baseline and no statistical variation across seeds. The claimed generalization to arbitrary configurations is assessed mostly by visually similar aggregate curves rather than matched configuration-wise errors or results on substantially out-of-distribution configurations.

The LLM evidence is weaker than the headline claims suggest. Table C.2 shows CoA-LoRA has higher perplexity than Q-LoRA in all three cases and is worse than LQ-LoRA, while the zero-shot table provides no dataset sample sizes, seeds, or uncertainty; its highly discretized values suggest a small evaluation sample. The amount of C4 data used is also unspecified despite claiming five epochs.

Efficiency reporting omits hardware, peak memory, search/evaluation overhead, quantization time, generator inference overhead, and deployment costs. Consequently, the claims of no additional time cost, real-time adaptation, and scalability are not adequately supported.

No code, detailed hyperparameter inventory, or precise data splits/subsampling protocol are provided, limiting reproducibility. Overall, the idea is promising, but the unresolved formulation errors and evaluation confounds prevent the evidence from supporting the central claims at a top-tier standard.

strengths: The problem is practically relevant: amortizing LoRA adaptation across heterogeneous quantization configurations could reduce deployment and fine-tuning costs.
The layer-wise r-by-r adjustment is a potentially useful lightweight parameterization, and combining configuration conditioning with configuration search is intuitively motivated.

The experiments cover four GLUE tasks, three model sizes up to 7B parameters, unseen configurations, multiple LoRA ranks, and several ablations. The manuscript is generally organized and readable. weaknesses: The configuration-search formulation contains serious technical inconsistencies. Equation 6 maximizes EHVI, but Equation 8 moves in the negative gradient direction, apparently minimizing it. Moreover, finite differences are taken with respect to learned configuration embeddings, yet adding or subtracting a unit vector need not correspond to any valid categorical quantization configuration; no projection or decoding procedure is defined.

The initialization in Appendix Equation 11 is dimensionally invalid: L1 has shape d-by-r and L2 has shape r-by-n, but the equation adds L1+L2 rather than multiplying them. More broadly, Algorithm 1 omits or ambiguously specifies assignment, reevaluation of newly generated configurations, GP refitting after the set changes, and maintenance of objective values. These issues prevent faithful implementation and undermine confidence in the reported method.

The central claim of supporting arbitrary configurations is overstated. Appendix A.2 instead searches for a configuration close to the final training set under an exact bit budget. The unseen-configuration experiment does not specify the split, number or sampling distribution of configurations, whether selection used the same procedure, or uncertainty across samples.

The evaluation is not controlled well enough to attribute improvements to the proposed adapter. CoA-LoRA performs task-specific configuration search using calibration performance, but there is no one-to-one Q-LoRA or LQ-LoRA baseline trained on the same searched configurations. Thus gains may arise from giving CoA-LoRA better configurations rather than from configuration-aware adjustment.

The hypervolume comparison is inadequately defined and potentially unfair. CoA-LoRA contributes roughly 50 points over 2.5–6.25 bits, whereas Q-LoRA and LQ-LoRA contribute only four points over 2.5–4 bits. The paper also inconsistently assigns performance, bit-width, accuracy, and perplexity to f1/f2, and does not clearly describe bit-width normalization. Hypervolume can therefore reward CoA-LoRA simply for having denser and broader coverage.

The large-language-model results do not substantiate the strongest performance claims. In Table C.2, CoA-LoRA has worse perplexity gaps than Q-LoRA on all three backbones, while LQ-LoRA improves over Q-LoRA. The zero-shot table evaluates only seven named tasks despite claiming eight, appears to use very small subsets given the coarse accuracy increments, and gives no sample sizes or uncertainty.

Reproducibility is insufficient: the architecture and embedding dimensions of the configuration-aware model, optimizer details, batch sizes, GP/kernel and acquisition settings, search iteration counts, dataset sampling, hardware, memory consumption, inference-generation overhead, random seeds, and code availability are missing. Training-time comparisons are consequently difficult to interpret.

Results are reported without multiple seeds, error bars, or statistical tests, even where differences are below one percentage point. Several explanations, such as the SST-2 generalization and segmentation behavior, are speculative rather than experimentally supported.

The appendix states that shared information lies mainly in L2 while configuration-specific information lies in L1, yet the proposed method transforms L2. This conflicts with the stated motivation and needs either correction or a controlled ablation comparing which factor is adjusted. Overall, the promising idea is not supported by a sufficiently sound specification or rigorous evaluation for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: supporting heterogeneous quantization budgets without fine-tuning and storing a separate LoRA adapter for every configuration.
The configuration-conditioned r×r transformation is a lightweight and intuitive way to amortize adaptation across layers and configurations.
The empirical scope is reasonably broad, covering four GLUE tasks, three generative LLMs from 1.5B to 7B parameters, multiple LoRA ranks, unseen configurations, and configuration-search ablations.

Reported results are promising: CoA-LoRA is generally competitive with configuration-specific Q-LoRA/LQ-LoRA while requiring substantially less aggregate training time, and it consistently improves over Shared-LoRA.
weaknesses: The central comparison is not fully controlled. CoA-LoRA searches for favorable configurations and evaluates roughly 50 points over 2.5–6.25 bits, whereas Q-LoRA and LQ-LoRA use only four points over 2.5–4 bits. Hypervolume therefore mixes adapter quality, configuration quality, coverage range, and number of evaluated solutions. Comparisons using exactly the same configurations and budgets are needed.

The configuration-search procedure is insufficiently specified and contains apparent mathematical inconsistencies. Finite-difference updates in a categorical, discrete configuration space are not mapped clearly back to valid choices; Eq. 8 subtracts the gradient sign despite maximizing EHVI; and relevant GP, embedding, and configuration-aware network details are absent.

Reproducibility and statistical evidence are weak: there are no multiple-seed results or error bars, hardware details, dataset/sample counts, complete optimization settings, or decomposition of search/evaluation overhead. The appendix's zero-shot scores appear highly discretized, but the evaluation sample size is not disclosed.

Several presentation errors undermine confidence: Eq. 11 adds the two LoRA factors instead of multiplying them, and Appendix C.1 says L2 is shared and L1 configuration-specific even though its correlation figure shows the opposite. The paper also lacks comparisons to conditional-adapter, hypernetwork, or weight-sharing/supernet approaches, and does not evaluate actual edge-device memory, latency, or deployment overhead.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: supporting heterogeneous quantization configurations without separately fine-tuning a LoRA adapter for every configuration.
The configuration-conditioned low-dimensional adjustment is intuitive and lightweight, and combining it with quantization-configuration search is a potentially useful systems/learning contribution.

The empirical scope is reasonably broad, covering RoBERTa-Large and language models from 1.5B to 13B parameters, multiple GLUE and zero-shot tasks, floating-point and integer mixed-precision quantization, and several LoRA ranks.

The paper includes useful ablations on configuration search, random configuration extension, unseen configurations, Pareto segmentation, and adapter rank. Reported results are often competitive with configuration-specific QLoRA/LQ-LoRA while reducing cumulative training time.
The presentation is generally organized, and the appendix provides architecture details, pseudocode, parameter counts, and additional results.
weaknesses: The central claim of adaptation to arbitrary configurations is insufficiently validated. The unseen-configuration experiment does not report the number or sampling distribution of unseen configurations, uncertainty across trials, or performance relative to a separately fine-tuned oracle on those same configurations. Appendix A.3 instead selects configurations close to the searched training set, which supports local interpolation more than arbitrary-configuration generalization.

The comparison conflates adapter generation with quantization-configuration optimization. CoA-LoRA is evaluated on configurations explicitly searched for high task performance, whereas configuration-specific baselines are shown at only a few bit budgets. Results on exactly matched configurations, including randomly sampled and adversarially distant configurations, are needed to establish that gains come from the proposed adapter adjustment rather than favorable configuration selection.

There is a serious internal inconsistency in the motivation for modifying L2. Section 4.2 says adaptation signal is concentrated in L2, while Appendix C.1 states that configuration-specific knowledge is primarily in L1 and shared information in L2. Moreover, the displayed correlation matrices appear to show high cross-configuration similarity for L1 and low similarity for L2, contradicting the appendix text. This undermines the stated empirical rationale for the core parameterization.

The discrete optimization procedure is under-specified and not mathematically convincing. A finite-difference step on a layer embedding does not directly define a valid move among categorical choices such as bit-width, data type, and bucket size; neither the projection/neighbor mapping nor boundary handling is described. GP scalability in a configuration space with hundreds of layer coordinates is also not analyzed.

The evaluation lacks statistical rigor: no random seeds, confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests are reported, despite several claimed improvements being small. Repeated search against calibration performance also creates overfitting risk, but the calibration/evaluation split, calibration-set size, and candidate-evaluation protocol are not adequately specified.

Efficiency claims are overstated. CoA-LoRA takes substantially longer than Shared-LoRA, and it is unclear whether reported time includes candidate quantization, repeated calibration evaluation, GP fitting, SVD initialization, and configuration search. No hardware, peak memory, energy, on-device latency, or adapter-generation latency is reported, despite edge deployment and 'no additional time cost' being central motivations.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a top-tier paper: the implementation link is missing, and important details such as C4 subset size, batch size, optimizer and schedule, number of search steps, GP kernel settings, reference-point construction, quantization implementation, and compute environment are absent. The claim of five C4 epochs within the reported times is especially difficult to interpret without the data subset and hardware.

The strongest evidence is concentrated on four GLUE classification tasks with one encoder model; the larger-model results mainly use perplexity or zero-shot evaluation after C4 adaptation. Instruction tuning, generative downstream tasks, and comparisons with stronger mixed-precision search or conditional-adapter baselines are missing. Overall, the promising idea is not yet supported with sufficiently controlled, reproducible evidence for acceptance.

strengths: The problem is practically relevant: supporting heterogeneous quantization configurations without independently fine-tuning an adapter for every deployment target could substantially reduce adaptation cost.
The layer-conditioned r-by-r transformation is lightweight, and combining it with configuration search is a reasonable design direction.
The empirical study covers several model sizes, GLUE and C4 evaluations, floating-point and integer mixed-precision settings, multiple LoRA ranks, unseen configurations, and some component ablations.
weaknesses: The central efficiency claim is not convincingly established. Every configuration still requires quantizing the model and computing configuration-specific SVD factors from the full-precision/quantized weight residual. The runtime, memory, storage, and on-device latency of these operations are excluded, making claims of "no additional time cost" and "real-time" arbitrary-configuration adaptation unsupported.

The comparison confounds adapter adaptation with configuration selection. CoA-LoRA searches configurations using task performance, whereas baseline configurations are generated through the reconstruction-based procedure in Eq. 11. Thus, its gains cannot be attributed specifically to the proposed configuration-aware adapter. A fair comparison would evaluate all adapters on identical configurations and separately quantify the benefit of configuration search.

The method is technically underspecified and internally inconsistent. Finite-difference steps in a learned embedding are not mapped clearly back to valid categorical quantization choices; Algorithm 1 fits the Gaussian process only once, omits evaluation/refitting after configuration updates, does not actually add updated configurations to C-prime, and contains an update without assignment. Equation 11 also adds L1 and L2 despite incompatible dimensions rather than using their product.

Evaluation reliability is weak. Results are apparently from single runs with no variance or statistical testing; the seen/unseen split, number and sampling distribution of unseen configurations, dataset subsets, optimizer, batch size, hardware, GP/kernel settings, and several search hyperparameters are missing. The implementation link is also incomplete.

Hypervolume comparisons are questionable because CoA-LoRA is evaluated densely over about 50 configurations while expensive baselines receive only five points. The paper also contradicts itself about whether larger or smaller HV is better. Direct matched-budget comparisons with equal evaluation density are needed.

The evidence cited as motivation is described inconsistently: the appendix claims shared information is concentrated in L2 and configuration-specific information in L1, while its correlation plots show much higher cross-configuration similarity for L1 than L2. This weakens confidence in both the explanation and presentation.

Generalization to "arbitrary" configurations is overstated. Inference selects configurations near the searched final set, and the unseen-configuration experiment lacks rigorous split details or comparisons against independently fine-tuned adapters on those unseen configurations.

Despite motivating edge deployment, the paper reports no actual device memory, throughput, energy, quantization-kernel support, or end-to-end deployment measurements. The custom 2/3/8-bit mixed configurations may not yield practical hardware speedups, so the claimed deployment impact remains speculative.

Novelty is moderate: the approach combines a small conditional transformation with established LoRA/SVD initialization and Bayesian multi-objective search, but it lacks either a strong theoretical result or sufficiently controlled empirical evidence to establish a top-tier contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses an important deployment problem: supporting heterogeneous quantization budgets without training and storing a separate LoRA adapter for every configuration.
The proposed layer-conditioned r×r transformation is lightweight relative to the backbone and is intuitively motivated as a way to avoid directly generating full adapter matrices.

The reported results are promising: CoA-LoRA generally improves over Shared-LoRA and often matches or exceeds configuration-specific QLoRA/LQ-LoRA while reporting lower aggregate training time.
The ablations on configuration search, rank, Pareto segmentation, unseen configurations, and configuration-set size help examine several important design choices.
weaknesses: The central optimization is not technically well specified and contains apparent errors. Equation 6 maximizes EHVI, but Equation 8 moves in the negative gradient direction. Moreover, finite differences C±δe are applied to discrete categorical configurations without defining a valid projection, and a layer embedding is treated as if it were a scalar coordinate. Algorithm 1 also does not clearly re-evaluate new configurations or refit the Gaussian process after the initial fit.

The SVD initialization is internally inconsistent. Equation 11 adds L1 and L2 although their dimensions differ and the preceding definition requires the product L1L2. The binary variable X is declared as N×κ with κ=5 configuration variables and constrained to choose one entry per layer, which does not represent the multi-valued Cartesian configuration space in Table 1. These issues make a core part of the method impossible to reproduce as written.

The stated motivation for adjusting L2 contradicts the appendix evidence. Appendix C.1 says shared components are in L2 and configuration-specific information is in L1, yet it then uses this to justify transforming L2; Figures C.1–C.2 appear to show high cross-configuration similarity for L1 and much lower similarity for L2. This inconsistency directly affects the architectural rationale.

The hypervolume comparison is insufficiently controlled. CoA-LoRA contributes roughly 50 densely sampled solutions, whereas QLoRA/LQ-LoRA are evaluated at only about five or six bit-widths; hypervolume can improve simply from denser coverage. The manuscript also inconsistently defines f1/f2, sometimes assigning f2 to bit-width and elsewhere to accuracy or perplexity, while the minimization formulation does not reconcile accuracy as a maximization objective.

The evaluation lacks uncertainty estimates, numbers of random seeds, complete split/sample-size details, and sufficiently detailed optimization settings. The zero-shot scores appear quantized in increments suggestive of very small evaluation subsets, but sample sizes are not disclosed. These omissions are material given that several reported improvements are small.

The efficiency claim is incomplete. Training time alone is reported, without peak memory, configuration-generation time, per-layer SVD cost, adapter-generation latency, quantization overhead, or real-device inference measurements. Since a new configuration apparently requires quantizing weights and computing residual SVDs, the strong claims of real-time or no-cost on-the-fly adaptation are not established.

Baseline fairness is unclear: CoA-LoRA jointly trains across many configurations and searches configurations using task feedback, while the one-to-one baselines are evaluated on a sparse set whose selection and total optimization budgets are not matched. A stronger comparison would use equal configuration sets, search budgets, data exposure, and wall-clock or compute budgets.

Although the empirical premise is interesting, the unresolved formulation errors, contradictory motivation, and insufficiently controlled evaluation prevent the current evidence from supporting acceptance at a top-tier venue. Corrected algorithms and equations, reproducible implementation details, equal-budget comparisons, multi-seed statistics, and end-to-end deployment measurements would be needed.
